titre: 1275: The English Law That Finally Says Who Can Be Bailed
accroche: In 1275, an English law set down in writing, for the first time, who could be released on bail before trial, and punished the sheriff who released anyone else.
contenu_vulgarise:
A man arrested in England before 1275 depended almost entirely on his county's sheriff to know whether he would await trial free or locked up. Nothing listed in writing which charges allowed release on bail, called mainprise, and which ruled it out. It was this uncertainty that the Statute of Westminster, enacted in 1275, set out to fill, in its fifteenth chapter: "Which Prisoners be mainpernable, and which not. The Penalty for unlawful Bailment."

## A codification, not an invention

The Statute of Westminster the First is not a text devoted solely to bail: it is a 51-chapter law, enacted at the first general Parliament held after the coronation of Edward I, a king who had returned from crusade in August 1274. Drafted largely by Robert Burnell, the king's chancellor, the text is written in Anglo-Norman French, the language of English law at the time, not in Latin. Its aim, according to Wikipedia, was to codify law that was already largely customary rather than create new law. The first chapter concerns free elections; the fifteenth chapter tackles a practice that had until then been left to local judgment: release before trial.

The text, available on the United Kingdom's official legislation website (legislation.gov.uk), distinguishes for the first time in writing the categories of prisoners who may be released on bail from those who may not, and sets a penalty for a sheriff who wrongly releases a non-bailable prisoner. The word "mainpernable" comes from mainprise, the undertaking by which a third party guarantees that the accused will appear at trial. Until then, this decision rested on the sheriff's own judgment, with no written rule to refer to and no penalty set for abuse.

## What the written rule shifts

The law did not create bail: mainprise already existed in practice. What it adds is a list and a penalty. From then on, a sheriff who releases a prisoner who should not have been released incurs his own liability; conversely, a defendant whose case fits the bailable categories has a written argument to make, rather than a favor to request. Chapter fifteen was applied in England and Wales until it was repealed by the Criminal Law Act 1826, and then by the Sheriffs Act 1887, which also repeals it in Ireland, alongside the Criminal Statutes (Ireland) Repeal Act 1828.

The statute as a whole did not disappear, though. Its fifth chapter, which forbids disturbing a free election by force or threat, remains in force in the United Kingdom today, seven hundred fifty years after its enactment. A single 1275 text can thus carry, chapter by chapter, provisions of very different ages: one repealed in the 19th century because its subject, pretrial release, was taken over by more detailed laws; another, on freedom to vote without coercion, still judged sufficient as written under a king who died in 1307.

carte.punch: In 1275, England wrote down, for the first time, who could leave prison before trial.
carte.idee: The Statute of Westminster of 1275, chapter fifteen, set down in writing who could be released on bail (mainprise) before trial and who could not, and punished a sheriff who released anyone else. Repealed in 1826, this rule sat alongside another chapter, on free elections, still in force today.

quiz.question: What does chapter fifteen of the Statute of Westminster 1275 add to the English practice of mainprise?
choix: A written list of which prisoners are bailable or not, and a penalty for a sheriff who wrongly releases one
The invention of bail, which did not exist before this law
A requirement that every defendant pay a fixed sum to be released
The transfer of this decision from sheriffs to royal itinerant judges alone
quiz.explication: Mainprise already existed before 1275 as a local practice left to the sheriff; the law adds a written list of the categories of prisoners concerned and a penalty for a sheriff who releases a prisoner who should not have been. It sets no fixed sum to pay and leaves the decision with sheriffs, not with itinerant judges alone.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Who drafted most of the Statute of Westminster 1275, and in what language?
choix: Robert Burnell, the king's chancellor, in Anglo-Norman French
King Edward I himself, in Latin
The sheriffs of each county, each in their own dialect
A board of itinerant judges, in Old English
quiz_supplementaire.explication: According to Wikipedia, the text was drafted largely by Robert Burnell, the king's chancellor, in Anglo-Norman French, the language of English law at the time, not in Latin. Neither the king himself, nor the sheriffs, nor a board of itinerant judges wrote it.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What repeals chapter fifteen of the Statute of Westminster 1275 in England and Wales?
choix: The Statute of Westminster 1285, which directly replaces it
Magna Carta, Article 17, on common pleas
The creation of the Court of Common Pleas in 1178
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Chapter fifteen is repealed in England and Wales by the Criminal Law Act 1826, then in Ireland by the Criminal Statutes (Ireland) Repeal Act 1828 and the Sheriffs Act 1887. There is no Statute of Westminster 1285 replacing it, and neither Magna Carta nor the Court of Common Pleas concerns pretrial release.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Which other chapter of the Statute of Westminster 1275 remains in force in the United Kingdom today?
choix: Chapter five, which forbids disturbing a free election by force
None: the 1275 law has been repealed in its entirety
The chapter setting allowed funeral expenses
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Chapter five, which forbids disturbing a free election by force or threat, remains in force in the United Kingdom. Chapter fifteen was repealed as early as the 19th century, so the 1275 law has not disappeared as a whole; and no chapter of this text concerns funeral expenses, a provision that belongs to the Roman Twelve Tables, not English law.
